ghawrath-sword.title: “Who will protect you from me?” — “Allah”: steadfastness under direct threat
participants: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
ghawrath-sword.eventDescription: During one of the expeditions, the Prophet ﷺ rested in the shade of a tree, hung his sword on it and slept. A bedouin came, took the sword and drew it, then woke the Prophet ﷺ standing over him with the sword and said: Who will protect you from me? The Prophet ﷺ answered with complete calm: “Allah.” The sword fell from the man's hand at the force of the moment; the Prophet ﷺ took it and did not punish him.
ghawrath-sword.historicalContext: One of the most dangerous moments for the Prophet's ﷺ own life, as he was alone and completely unarmed at the moment of the threat.
ghawrath-sword.problemType: Facing a direct threat and real danger to one's life at a moment of weakness or isolation
ghawrath-sword.responseType: Complete calm without panic, answering with certainty about the true source of safety, then forgiving once the danger passed
emotionsAddressed: Panic under a direct threat to life
The urge for revenge after surviving a real danger that threatened you personally
principles: True steadfastness appears at the moment of direct danger, not only after it passes
Certainty in Allah is a source of calm even at moments of apparent weakness
Forgiving someone who actually tried to harm you is a very high degree of self-control
modernApplications: In moments of real danger or threat, focus on your inner source of steadiness instead of giving in to full panic
After surviving a situation that could have badly harmed you, do not let the desire for revenge govern your next reaction
Remember that feeling outwardly weak does not mean all strength or safety is gone
notToApplyTo: This does not mean not taking security measures or reasonable caution in dangerous situations; the steadiness here is inner, not neglect of precaution
behaviorObservations: He answered with one confident word, without hesitation or fearful bargaining
He did not punish the man after the sword fell from his hand and the danger was over
whatToAvoid: Confusing inner steadiness with neglecting precautions and real means of safety
ghawrath-sword.reflection: The hardest test of steadfastness is not when danger is absent, but the moment it stands directly over your head.
keywords: i was directly threatened and was terrified
how to act in real danger to my life
i survived a dangerous situation and want revenge on the one who threatened me

hadithRefs.narrator: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with them)

contrasts: There: a danger anticipated and prepared for by hiding; here: a sudden danger at the weakest moment — and in both, the same steadfastness

da'in-jamal-afdal.title: “The one with a right may speak”: when the claimant is rude but right
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
da'in-jamal-afdal.eventDescription: A man came to demand a debt the Prophet ﷺ owed him, and spoke roughly and harshly. The Companions were about to deal severely with him because of his manner. The Prophet ﷺ stopped them and said: “Leave him, for the one who has a right is entitled to speak.” Then he ordered that a camel be bought for him like the one he had borrowed; they could only find one better and older, and he said: “Buy it and give it to him, for the best of you are those who repay best.”
da'in-jamal-afdal.historicalContext: One of the foundational hadith on financial dealings and repaying debts well; agreed to be authentic.
da'in-jamal-afdal.problemType: Dealing with someone who demands a right genuinely owed, but in a rude or provocative way
da'in-jamal-afdal.responseType: Stopping those around you from taking your side against the rightful claimant, then paying the right in full and even better
emotionsAddressed: The urge to ignore the right of someone who claimed it badly
The temptation to use the claimant's bad manners as an excuse to fall short in their right
principles: A bad manner of claiming does not cancel the right itself or justify falling short in it
Someone owed by you may show some harshness in claiming, and this does not always deserve punishment
Repaying a right well is a stronger moral message than just paying the minimum
modernApplications: If someone rudely demands what you genuinely owe, do not let your annoyance at their manner delay giving them their right
Stop those around you from escalating against someone who is right just because they disliked his manner
If you can pay more than the minimum required, there is real moral good in it
behaviorObservations: He stopped his Companions from escalating against the man despite his harshness
He ordered that he be given better than he was owed, not just the minimum
He gave a general principle as the reason: the best of you are those who repay best
whatToAvoid: Confusing judgement of the claimant's manner with the basis of what he is owed
da'in-jamal-afdal.reflection: When the one in authority clearly separates a person's right from their manner, justice becomes a standard that bad manners cannot shake.
keywords: someone demands what i owe in a rude way
how to separate someone's right from their bad manner
should i delay paying someone because he spoke harshly

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: Here he was patient with the rudeness of someone with a clear right; there he strongly reproached someone who erred with good intentions towards the weak — the measure is the act's effect, not the doer's intention alone

usama-shahada.title: “Did you split open his heart?”: judging an intention you cannot see
participants: Usamah ibn Zayd (may Allah be pleased with him)
usama-shahada.eventDescription: In one battle, Usamah ibn Zayd pursued an enemy fighter. When he overtook him with his weapon, the man pronounced the testimony of faith. But Usamah thought he said it out of fear of the weapon, not true belief, and killed him. When this reached the Prophet ﷺ he reproached him severely and repeatedly: “Did you kill him after he said ‘There is no god but Allah’?” Usamah excused himself saying the man said it out of fear of the weapon. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Did you split open his heart to know whether he meant it or not?” He kept repeating the reproach until Usamah wished he had only embraced Islam after that day, so deeply was he affected.
usama-shahada.historicalContext: An extremely serious wartime situation, teaching a fundamental principle of not judging hidden intentions based on suspicion, even in the hardest circumstances.
usama-shahada.problemType: Judging someone's intention or the truth of their words based on a guess or suspicion, however logical it seemed at the time
usama-shahada.responseType: Severe, repeated reproach for using suspicion as the basis for judging what is in another person's heart
emotionsAddressed: Overconfidence in your ability to know someone's intention from appearances or circumstances
Justifying a harsh judgement of someone based on your reading of their motives, not their words
principles: No one can know what is in people's hearts, however logical their reading of motives seems
An outward declaration counts, even if someone doubts the sincerity of the speaker
Severe, repeated reproach is an educational method when the principle violated is very grave
modernApplications: Before judging someone's intention or honesty based on your own reading of their situation, remember you cannot know what is inside them
Take people's statements at face value unless you have clear evidence, not just suspicion
If you misjudged someone's intention based on suspicion, accept correction as a chance to learn, not an insult
notToApplyTo: This is an exceptional and extremely serious context; the general principle applies everywhere, but the severity of the reproach fits the gravity of this particular situation
behaviorObservations: He repeated the reproach several times to stress the gravity of the principle, not merely to scold
He did not just name the mistake, but explained the principle behind it
whatToAvoid: Applying the severity of this reproach to every simple everyday situation; the gravity of this context is exceptional
usama-shahada.reflection: One of the deepest lessons of this situation is that the gravest injustice can come from a suspicion that seemed entirely logical to its holder at the time.
keywords: i judged someone's intention and was wrong
how to stop interpreting other people's intentions
do i have the right to judge someone's sincerity from my suspicion alone

hadithRefs.narrator: Usamah ibn Zayd (may Allah be pleased with them)

contrasts: In the first he forgave after asking about the motive; in the second he rejected assuming one can know the motive at all — both reject hasty judgement from different angles
Repeated patience with an enemy until his heart changed, versus immediate, severe reproach for presuming bad intent in another enemy — the difference is in verification, not in the basis of mercy

bukaa-tifl-salat.title: “Not wanting to make it hard for his mother”: changing your plan for someone who cannot see you
participants: Abu Qatadah al-Harith ibn Rib‘i (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
bukaa-tifl-salat.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ would sometimes begin a prayer intending to make it long, but if he heard the crying of an infant with its mother in the rows, he would lighten and shorten his prayer. He explained the reason himself: “Not wanting to make things hard for his mother,” meaning he did not want the mother's heart to be troubled by her crying child while she was trying to pray.
bukaa-tifl-salat.historicalContext: One of the hadith showing the Prophet's ﷺ fine attention to the circumstances of worshippers, especially women who attended prayer with their children.
prophetTraits: Considering those he could not directly see
bukaa-tifl-salat.problemType: Holding on to a plan or prior intention even when something appears that calls for changing it out of consideration for someone else
bukaa-tifl-salat.responseType: Changing the plan at once out of deep empathy with another person's experience that they had not expressed directly
emotionsAddressed: Holding to a personal plan despite its unintended negative effect on others
Not noticing someone else's experience because they did not complain openly
principles: Deep empathy means imagining someone else's experience even if they asked nothing of you
Changing a plan or decision out of consideration for others is maturity, not inconsistency
You may have every right to do something, but considering others may matter more than using your right in full
modernApplications: Watch the effect of your plans or decisions on those around you, even if they do not complain openly
Do not hold to a prior plan if something appears that calls for adjusting it out of consideration for someone's feelings
Remember that having the full right to something does not mean using it fully is always the best choice
behaviorObservations: He changed his plan as soon as he heard the child crying
He explained his motive clearly himself: not wanting to burden the mother, not annoyance at the child's noise
whatToAvoid: Thinking that considering others means giving up every personal plan or goal without any measure
bukaa-tifl-salat.reflection: The highest level of empathy is to see a suffering no one complained of, and change your behaviour for it without being asked.
keywords: should i change my plan out of consideration for someone's feelings
how to be more empathetic with those around me without being asked
considering others' feelings in daily decisions

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Qatadah al-Harith ibn Rib‘i (may Allah be pleased with him)

janazat-yahudi.title: “Was it not a soul?”: humanity above religious difference
subCategories: Dealing with people of other faiths
participants: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
janazat-yahudi.eventDescription: A funeral passed by the Prophet ﷺ and he stood up for it out of respect. He was told: O Messenger of Allah, it is the funeral of a Jew. He answered with a brief, deep sentence: “Was it not a soul?”, showing that respect for human dignity in death does not depend on a person's religion or belief.
janazat-yahudi.historicalContext: One of the brief but highly meaningful hadith on respecting humanity regardless of religious difference. Scholars later discussed whether the specific ruling of standing for a funeral continued, but this does not affect the core principle the words express.
janazat-yahudi.problemType: Treating the tragedy or death of someone of a different religion or belief with disregard or indifference
janazat-yahudi.responseType: A brief sentence establishing that human dignity is a foundation that comes before every difference of belief
emotionsAddressed: Inner disregard for the tragedy or pain of someone religiously different from you
Believing that human respect is conditional on agreement in belief
principles: Human dignity in life and death does not depend on religion or belief
Deep differences of belief do not cancel basic human empathy
Sometimes the deepest principles are summed up in the shortest words
modernApplications: Express human sympathy for the tragedy or loss of someone who differs from you in religion or thought, as you would with someone who shares your belief
Review any inner tendency to lessen the value of someone's pain just because they differ from you
Remember that basic human respect comes before every intellectual or religious disagreement
behaviorObservations: He answered with a brief rhetorical question that sums up a deep principle without elaboration
whatToAvoid: Turning this principle into rigid legal details instead of focusing on its human essence
janazat-yahudi.reflection: Sometimes the deepest lessons of humanity need no long sermon, but one sincere phrase: Was it not a soul?
keywords: how to respond to the death of someone of another religion
is respect for humanity conditional on religion
condolences to someone of a different religion

hadithRefs.narrator: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with them)

yusuf-ikhwa.title: Yusuf and his brothers: “No blame upon you today”
yusuf-ikhwa.eventDescription: Yusuf's brothers envied him for their father's love of him, so they threw him into a well as a child and lied to their father. Years passed: he was sold as a slave, falsely accused, and imprisoned for several years; then Allah established him in authority over the storehouses of Egypt. His brothers came to him in need without recognising him. When he made himself known and they admitted their wrong, he said: “No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you.” Later, when the family was reunited, he mentioned his release from prison but not the well, and attributed what had happened to Satan having caused discord between him and his brothers.
yusuf-ikhwa.historicalContext: A complete story in Surah Yusuf, which Allah called “the best of stories”, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah in the Year of Sorrow as consolation. The Prophet ﷺ quoted these words of Yusuf on the day of the conquest of Makkah, with Quraysh.
yusuf-ikhwa.problemType: Betrayal or serious harm from siblings or relatives out of jealousy, and then the need to decide how to relate to them years later
yusuf-ikhwa.responseType: Long patience, then complete forgiveness when able, while preserving the dignity of those who erred and not exposing them
emotionsAddressed: Pain from betrayal by those closest
principles: Harm from those closest hurts more, but forgiving them carries greater reward
True forgiveness does not include taunting or constantly reminding of the mistake
Saving face for the one who erred after he admits it is part of complete forgiveness
Admission of fault by the other side opens the door to reconciliation
Attributing the rift to Satan's interference helps both sides turn the page without humiliation
modernApplications: If there is an old wound between you and your brother or sister, ask yourself: am I waiting for an apology in a certain form, or is a general admission enough?
When reconciling, avoid bringing up painful details in front of others, as Yusuf did not mention the well
Pay attention to the roots of jealousy in the family (favouritism, comparison) and work on treating them, not punishing their results
If Allah one day gives you power over someone who hurt you, remember that moment is a test for you, not for them
notToApplyTo: Forgiveness does not mean handing yourself over to someone who is still harming you; Yusuf forgave after they admitted it and had changed
If family harm is ongoing or serious (violence, financial exploitation), protection and boundaries come first
behaviorObservations: Yusuf was patient for many years without letting his pain turn into a grudge that steered his life
He did not use his position and power for revenge when his brothers came to him in need
He forgave with a decisive word, “today”, meaning: it is over from this moment
He did good to them after forgiving, asking for the whole family to be brought, not just dropping punishment
He avoided mentioning the well in public to spare his brothers' feelings
whatToAvoid: Forgiving in words while continuing to hint at and recall the mistake at every occasion
Turning every family gathering into a trial of the past
yusuf-ikhwa.reflection: The greatest victory is to have the power to take revenge on the one who broke you, and to choose to say: No blame upon you today.
keywords: my siblings are jealous of me
my sister is jealous of me
my father favours me so my siblings hate me
my siblings hurt me in the past

quranRefs.context: Yusuf said it to his brothers after they recognised him and admitted their wrong: “By Allah, certainly has Allah preferred you over us, and indeed, we have been sinners”
quranRefs.relevance: Complete forgiveness at the moment of full power: no taunting, no reminding, no conditions

quranRefs.context: When the whole family gathered in Egypt
quranRefs.relevance: High emotional intelligence: he avoided mentioning the well so as not to hurt his brothers, and attributed the rift to Satan, not to evil in them

contrasts: The Prophet ﷺ recalled Yusuf's very words on the day of the conquest of Makkah: forgiveness at full power, this time with Quraysh

yaqub-huzn.title: Ya‘qub: “I only complain of my suffering and grief to Allah”
yaqub-huzn.eventDescription: Ya‘qub lost his son Yusuf for many years, then lost his second son Binyamin, and his grief grew so intense that his eyes turned white with sorrow. When his sons blamed him for mentioning Yusuf so much, he said: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.” Then he told them to search: “Go and find out about Yusuf and his brother, and despair not of relief from Allah.”
yaqub-huzn.historicalContext: From the Makkan Surah Yusuf. Ya‘qub was a noble prophet, yet he did not hide his grief and was not blamed for it; rather, Allah praised his patience.
yaqub-huzn.problemType: Prolonged grief over losing a loved one (death, absence, estrangement), with those around blaming the continuing grief
yaqub-huzn.responseType: Complaining to Allah alone, keeping hope alive, and continuing to strive
principles: Grief is not a lack of faith, and weeping is a mercy Allah placed in hearts
There is a difference between complaining to Allah (worship) and resenting Allah's decree (blameworthy)
Hope in Allah's mercy is a duty however long the time
True hope translates into practical steps
modernApplications: Do not force yourself to hide your grief in front of people to look “strong”; allow yourself to grieve and give it time with Allah
If others blame you for how long you grieve, you need not defend yourself; it is enough to say: I complain to Allah
Give your grief an outlet in supplication and prostration instead of bottling it up until it becomes illness
Look for the “finding out” in your life: a small step that brings back some hope and movement
notToApplyTo: If grief turns into depression that disrupts daily life (sleep, eating, work) for weeks, seeking professional help is taking the means
behaviorObservations: He expressed his sorrow honestly — “Oh, my sorrow over Yusuf” — without pretence
He kept his complaint for Allah and did not complain of Allah's decree to people
His hope stayed alive despite the years, resting on his knowledge of Allah
He turned hope into a practical instruction to his sons to search
whatToAvoid: Blaming the grieving for their grief or rushing them to “get over” the loss
Turning hope into passive waiting with no effort
yaqub-huzn.reflection: You were not asked not to grieve, but to know to whom you bring your grief.
keywords: i can't get over the loss
people blame me for my grief
i miss the one i lost
my son travelled and doesn't call

quranRefs.relevance: Intense grief and weeping contradict neither prophethood nor patience
Complaining to Allah is legitimate, even worship; what is blameworthy is complaining about Allah to people
True hope is practical: it drives searching and effort, not passive waiting

yunus-hut.title: Yunus in the belly of the whale: saved by admission, not justification
participants: Yunus (peace be upon him), Dhu al-Nun
yunus-hut.eventDescription: Yunus left his people in anger before Allah had permitted him, and boarded a ship. Its passengers cast lots, the lot fell on him, he was thrown into the sea and the whale swallowed him. In three darknesses — the night, the sea and the whale's belly — he called out: “There is no god except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers.” Allah answered him and saved him from distress.
yunus-hut.historicalContext: His story is told in Surahs al-Anbiya', al-Saffat, al-Qalam and Yunus. The Prophet ﷺ said that no Muslim ever makes this supplication for anything without Allah answering him.
yunus-hut.problemType: Falling into distress or crisis partly of one's own making through a hasty decision or anger, with a feeling of darkness and being closed in
yunus-hut.responseType: Declaring Allah's oneness, glorifying Him, sincerely admitting the mistake, then awaiting relief
principles: Admitting a mistake is the beginning of getting out of a crisis, not a sign of weakness
There is no darkness deeper than Yunus's three, yet his supplication reached
A decision made in anger may lead into a trap, and returning to Allah repairs it
Glorification with admission: the fault is mine, not Allah's decree
modernApplications: If you are in trouble because of a hasty decision, start by admitting it to yourself and to Allah without excessive self-punishment
Repeat the supplication of Dhu al-Nun in every distress; the Prophet ﷺ promised it would be answered
Do not wait to get out of the crisis to return to Allah; return to Him while you are in the middle of it
Separate “I made a mistake” (useful admission) from “I am a failure and deserve nothing” (destructive self-punishment)
notToApplyTo: Admitting a mistake before Allah does not mean bearing other people's sins, or accepting unjust blame
behaviorObservations: He began his supplication by declaring Allah's oneness before asking
He did not ask for anything explicitly, but admitted and glorified — the most eloquent request
He did not blame his people or the ship's passengers, but attributed the wrong to himself
whatToAvoid: Drowning in blaming others or circumstances during a crisis
Despairing that supplication can reach from the depths of distress
yunus-hut.reflection: From the belly of the whale, in three darknesses, a sincere word reached the heavens; no place is too far for Allah to hear you.
keywords: the world closed in on me
i made a mistake and ruined my life

quranRefs.context: In the belly of the whale
quranRefs.relevance: Admitting personal fault without justification or blaming others
“And thus do We save the believers” extends the promise to every believer in distress

hadithRefs.narrator: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him)

ayyub-sabr.title: Ayyub: long patience through illness and loss
ayyub-sabr.eventDescription: Ayyub was tested in his body, wealth and children over a long time, and he was patient and hoped for reward; no resentment is reported from him. Then he called his Lord with refinement: “Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.” Allah answered him, removed his affliction, gave him back his family and the like of them with them, and praised him: “Indeed, We found him patient — an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one repeatedly turning back.”
ayyub-sabr.historicalContext: His story is told in Surahs al-Anbiya' and Sad. Details of the length of the trial in commentary books include many unreliable narrations from earlier traditions; what is established is what is in the Quran.
ayyub-sabr.problemType: A long or chronic illness, or a series of losses that drain body and soul
ayyub-sabr.responseType: Patience with courteous supplication, remembering Allah's mercy, and taking the means
principles: Complaining to Allah does not contradict patience
A long trial is not proof of Allah's anger
Relief may come through simple means after a long wait (“strike the ground with your foot”)
The sick person receives the reward of their usual deeds even when unable to do them
modernApplications: Phrase your supplication honestly about your state — “O Lord, adversity has touched me” — without shame at showing your weakness before Allah
Keep to medical treatment regularly; Ayyub himself was told to take a means: “Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink”
Remember that worship you cannot do because of illness is recorded for you in full
Find someone to accompany you through the trial, and do not isolate yourself
notToApplyTo: Patience does not mean abandoning treatment or neglecting medical means
behaviorObservations: He called his Lord in the form of a statement, not an objection
He appealed to Allah's most expansive attribute: mercy
He responded to Allah's command to take a simple means
whatToAvoid: Interpreting illness as inevitable punishment for a sin
Despairing of healing or of reward
ayyub-sabr.reflection: Ayyub did not say “Why me?”, but “Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful” — and the complaint itself became worship.
keywords: why is all this happening to me

quranRefs.context: His supplication after a long trial
quranRefs.relevance: The manners of complaint: describing one's state and appealing to Allah's mercy without objection
Complaining to Allah did not remove him from the description of the patient

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them)

musa-firawn.title: Musa before Pharaoh: “Fear not, indeed I am with you both”
subCategories: Fear of facing someone in authority
musa-firawn.eventDescription: Allah commanded Musa to go to the tyrant Pharaoh, and Musa did not hide his fears: he asked for his chest to be expanded, his task made easy and the knot in his tongue untied, and asked that his brother Harun be with him as a helper. Then they both said: “Indeed, we are afraid that he will hasten punishment against us or that he will transgress.” The answer came: “Fear not. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see,” and Allah commanded them: “Speak to him with gentle speech, that perhaps he may be reminded or fear.”
musa-firawn.historicalContext: In Surah Ta-Ha, at the start of Musa's mission after returning from Madyan; he had earlier left Egypt in fear after accidentally killing a man.
musa-firawn.problemType: Fear of facing someone in authority (a manager, an official, a strict parent) or of speaking in front of people
musa-firawn.responseType: Admitting the fear, asking for an expanded chest, choosing a helper, and confronting with gentle speech
principles: Fear does not mean being unfit for the task; even the prophets feared
Knowing your weak points and asking for someone to complement them is wisdom
Gentle speech is more effective even with the harshest people
Allah's presence is the greatest source of calm
modernApplications: Before a hard meeting, interview or presentation, repeat Musa's supplication: “My Lord, expand for me my chest and ease for me my task”
Identify your weak point (speaking, nerves) and ask for help with it, as Musa asked for Harun
Prepare your words and begin gently and calmly even if the other side is domineering
Remember that courage is doing what is right while afraid, not having the fear disappear
notToApplyTo: Gentleness in manner does not mean giving up the right or the substance
behaviorObservations: He did not pretend to be strong but declared his fear to Allah
He asked for exactly what he needed: an open chest, an easy task, eloquent speech and a helper
He kept to gentle speech in his confrontation
whatToAvoid: Running away from the task because of fear
musa-firawn.reflection: As long as Allah hears and sees, you are not alone in any room you enter.
keywords: i'm afraid to speak in front of people

quranRefs.relevance: Admitting weak points and asking Allah for help with them
Natural fear is not blamed; its cure is remembering that Allah is with you
Courage does not mean harshness; even with a tyrant one begins gently
